sections.h2: Untreated cotton stalk gives about a third of paddy straw's gas per tonne

chart.title: Only pretreatment brings cotton stalk near paddy straw, and only in the lab
chart.sub: kg of CBG per tonne of residue. Cotton rows are this blog's lab-based estimates.
chart.source: Kulkarni and Shastri (2025); Verbio Lehragaga; Zhang et al. (2018); this blog's estimates.

sections.means: Untreated cotton stalk yields about 33 kg of CBG a tonne, against about 100 to 120 kg for paddy straw at Verbio's plant.
sections.todo: Test pretreated cotton stalk at a working plant before counting on the pretreated revenue figure.

sections.h2: Cotton stalk yields the least methane of the field residues tested

chart.title: Even pretreated, cotton stalk gives less methane than every other residue listed
chart.sub: mL of methane per gram of volatile solids, pretreated values from laboratory batch tests.
chart.source: Zhang et al. (2018); Song et al. (2013); Victorin et al. (2020); You et al. (2013); Song et al. (2014); Formann et al. (2020); Janke et al. (2017).

sections.means: After the most effective pretreatment, cotton stalk reaches 192 millilitres of methane per gram, below every other residue in the table.
sections.todo: Digest cotton stalk alongside dung or another nitrogen-rich feed, since its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio is high.

sections.h2: None of the eleven north Indian CBG plants studied used cotton stalk

chart.title: Dung and press mud feed the plants; cotton stalk feeds none
chart.sub: Number of the eleven plants using each feedstock, per TERI's January 2025 study.
chart.source: TERI for the Global Methane Initiative (January 2025).

sections.means: Plants run on dung and press mud because those are wet, digest easily and sit at one site, while cotton stalk is dry and scattered.
sections.todo: Pair any cotton-stalk plant with dung, and collect and shred stalks promptly so they do not carry pink bollworm.
